record.paper_title: Open Problems in Applying Random-Matrix Theory to Nuclear Reactions
record.context_brief: s-wave neutron channels in GOE scattering theory
record.original_question: How can the standard GOE scattering formulation with a fixed number Λ of open channels and an energy-independent coupling matrix W be given an adequate theoretical treatment for experimentally relevant s-wave neutron channels, where neither an angular-momentum barrier nor a Coulomb barrier suppresses coupling to GOE states and the fixed-channel approximation over a finite energy interval can be most strongly violated?

evidence.quote: The number Λ of open channels in Eqs. (4, 5) is considered fixed. With increasing energy, the number of open channels in any nuclear reaction actually increases exponentially. Therefore, Eqs. (4, 5) provide a useful approximation to S only within some finite energy interval ∆E.

The assumption is most strongly violated by s-wave neutron channels because here neither angular momentum barrier nor Coulomb barrier suppress the coupling to the GOE states. It seems that the number of such cases that are experimentally relevant, is small. Their adequate theoretical treatment would pose a problem.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the standard Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) formulation of compound-nucleus scattering. Let H be an N×N real symmetric random matrix drawn from the GOE, representing the internal Hamiltonian of the compound system. Let Λ be a fixed positive integer denoting the number of open channels, and let W be a real N×Λ coupling matrix whose entries are taken to be energy-independent. The scattering matrix is defined by

   S_{ab}(E) = δ_{ab} − 2π i [W^T (E·I_N − H + iπ W W^T)^{-1} W]_{ab},   a,b = 1,…,Λ.

In actual nuclear reactions the number of open channels grows (roughly exponentially) with the energy E, so the fixed-Λ, energy-independent-W form above can serve as an approximation to the true S-matrix only over some finite energy interval ΔE. The fixed-channel approximation is most severely violated for s-wave neutron channels, since for these channels there is neither an angular-momentum centrifugal barrier nor a Coulomb barrier to suppress the coupling between the entrance channel and additional open channels associated with the GOE states across a wide energy range.

Problem. Develop a theoretical framework that extends the GOE scattering formalism above to give an adequate description of s-wave neutron channels, properly accounting for the fact that the number of effective open channels and the channel couplings vary significantly with energy across the relevant interval, so that statistical observables (such as cross-section autocorrelation functions, S-matrix moments, and resonance-width distributions) can be computed in a way that remains accurate when the fixed-Λ, energy-independent-W approximation breaks down.
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted search did not surface any work providing a complete random-matrix-theoretic treatment of s-wave neutron channels with energy-dependent open-channel number and couplings. Related work on Porter–Thomas deviations and coupled-channels neutron-nucleus scattering exists, but no resolution of the specific GOE formulation problem was found, so the problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Neutron Resonance Widths and the Porter-Thomas Distribution
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses dynamical effects that violate orthogonal invariance and cause deviations from the Porter-Thomas distribution related to the GOE.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work on s-wave neutron resonances explores deviations from GOE predictions but does not provide a full energy-dependent-channel GOE scattering treatment.

status_evidence.title: Coupled-channels calculations for nuclear reactions
status_evidence.snippet: The coupled-channels method treats couplings to excited states to all orders, but is a deterministic optical-model framework rather than a GOE statistical extension.
status_evidence.claim: Existing coupled-channels approaches address energy-dependent couplings phenomenologically but not within a random-matrix framework for s-wave neutrons.
